findings.detail: If LGR vests on 1 April 2028 as originally intended, the Secretary of State may issue Section 24 directions that could restrict capital projects. findings.matters: Lenders need to understand potential constraints on the council's capital spending that could affect asset maintenance and service delivery; this creates uncertainty around project completion and timing.

findings.headline: Three million pounds set aside in reserves for Local Government Reorganisation implementation, with allocation still being determined
findings.detail: The council has set aside £3.0m in reserves to cover transitional costs related to LGR implementation. The work to allocate these funds to specific purposes is ongoing. This reduces reserves available to support the revenue budget.
findings.matters: A material one-off provision drawn from reserves reduces the available buffer for future budget shortfalls and compounds the reserve sustainability challenge identified in the MTFP.

findings.headline: Managed vacancy factor of £250k cannot be achieved due to high staff retention, requiring review
findings.detail: The council budgeted for £250k in savings from managed vacancies (not filling vacancies to save money). However, staff retention has been higher than expected, preventing the council from achieving this saving. The factor will be reviewed.
findings.matters: If budgeted vacancy savings cannot be achieved, this indicates a structural overspend in payroll that must be addressed through other savings, service changes, or accepted as higher than planned costs.

findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget assumed a 3% pay award. Pay negotiations have resulted in a calculated settlement of 3.8%, which is 0.8 percentage points higher. This increase is subject to final agreement with UNISON.
findings.matters: Pay is typically 50%+ of a council's budget; a 0.8% variance on a large payroll base is material and must be funded from elsewhere or accepted as an overspend.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: A one per cent change in average interest rates could swing annual investment income by more than £1m, with rates currently higher than originally budgeted
findings.detail: The council's budget includes projected investment income based on assumed interest rates and available balances. In the current economic climate, interest rates are remaining higher than expected when the 2026/27 budget was set. This creates material income volatility: a 1% movement in average rates could change annual investment income by more than £1m.
findings.matters: Investment income is a material component of budget balance; this volatility creates material planning risk and could require compensating savings if rates fall, or enable additional spending if rates rise.
findings.figures: £1m+ per 1% interest rate change
findings.quote: In the changing economic climate interest rates are continuing to remain higher than expected and by way of illustration, a one per cent change in the average interest rate on investments could result in more than a £1 million change in investment income over a year.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant declining from £4.29m to £3.36m by 2028/29, with no transitional protection in place
findings.detail: The provisional local government settlement provided figures through 2028/29. Revenue Support Grant will decline by approximately £936k over two years. The council notes that no transitional protection is in place and it is not on the funding floor, meaning it is fully exposed to this reduction.
findings.matters: Declining core government funding worsens the structural budget deficit and reduces the council's flexibility to address budget gaps; no protection means the impact falls entirely on the council's own resources or services.
findings.quote: The provisional local government settlement for 2026/27 was announced in December 2025 and provided provisional figures for 2027/28 and 2028/29, it is expected that these figures will be broadly confirmed in December 2026. findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan projected reserve depletion exceeding sustainable parameters from 2027/28, with gap widening to £4.8m by 2030/31
findings.detail: The February 2026 MTFP projected reserves would be used at £3.6m in 2027/28 against a sustainable level of £2.9m, creating a £754k shortfall. This gap grows to £2.1m by 2028/29 and £4.8m by 2030/31. The LGR pause means the council now faces addressing this sooner than initially expected.
findings.matters: This indicates a structural budget deficit requiring significant service reductions or increased income; the deteriorating trajectory raises creditworthiness concerns and signals urgent need for action.
findings.quote: the amount expected to be used in 2027/28 was much higher than that needed in 2026/27 and would not be in line with the recommended parameters, based on current estimates. Beyond 2027/28 the use of reserves was projected to continue to be unsustainable and outside of the parameters set, and action will be required by the council to address the increasing budget gap.

findings.paper_title: VALE Cabinet budget setting report Oct 2026
findings.headline: Government paused Local Government Reorganisation on 7 September 2026, leaving uncertain whether Vale will be replaced from 1 April 2028 as originally planned or later
findings.detail: The council had expected to be abolished and replaced by Ridgeway/Greater Oxford unitary councils from April 2028. The government paused the LGR process on 7 September 2026, placing under review the minded-to decision. The council now assumes it will likely still exist in 2028/29 but the timing is uncertain—it could be April 2028, April 2029, or later.
findings.matters: A lender or peer council needs to understand whether the council will continue to exist and for how long, as this affects planning horizon and whether long-term financial solutions are required.
findings.figures: LGR vesting originally planned 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Whilst it is now considered most likely that Vale will still exist in – and will therefore be required to set a budget for – 2028/29, it is not out of the question that the original vesting day of the new unitary could be 1 April 2028 as originally envisaged or be later than 1 April 2029.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Vale Treasury activities 2025-26
findings.headline: Treasury investment interest income of £8.1 million exceeded original budget of £4.3 million in 2025-26 due to sustained high interest rates and larger cash balances
findings.detail: Section 5 reports actual interest earned of £8.1 million against a budgeted £4.3 million, a favorable variance of approximately £2.1 million (49 per cent). Section 6 attributes this outperformance to sustained levels of higher interest rates throughout the year and cash balances higher than forecast. The council's average daily investment balance was £188 million during the year.
findings.matters: Material favorable variance in treasury income is significant for lenders assessing financial stability and cash generation capacity, and for peer councils forecasting treasury income. However, the favorable variance appears driven primarily by the high interest rate environment of 2025-26, which has since declined materially, suggesting this level of outperformance may not recur.

findings.paper_title: Joint AGC outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Neither council required borrowing during 2025/26
findings.detail: Both councils operated without need to access debt markets during the year. The prudential framework provides flexibility to borrow short-term for cash flow if future needs arise, but no such need materialized.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial stability partly through debt activity and cash management. The absence of unplanned borrowing signals healthy cash reserves and financial resilience.
findings.figures: No borrowing activity recorded in 2025/26; prudential limits set but not accessed
findings.quote: During 2025/26, there has not been a need for either council to borrow and both councils continue to take a prudent approach to their debt strategy.

findings.paper_title: Joint AGC outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Interest rate forecasts show Base Rate static through 2026, with declines not expected until Q3 2027
findings.detail: MUFG Corporate Markets (the councils' treasury advisors) forecast interest rates will remain unchanged for the whole of 2026, with no declines expected until Q3 2027. Volatility from Middle East conflict and energy-driven inflation could push rates higher than the base case.
findings.matters: The benign interest rate environment that drove 2025/26 outperformance is ending. Finance directors need to budget for lower returns on investments in 2026/27, affecting revenue assumptions in medium-term financial plans.
findings.figures: Base Rate at 3.75% in March 2026; no rate movement forecast through 2026

findings.paper_title: Joint AGC outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Both councils exceeded treasury investment budgets in 2025/26 as interest rate cuts proved slower than forecast
findings.detail: The Treasury Management Strategy forecast Bank Rate would reach 3.75% by Q1 2025/26, but rates instead fell more gradually—three 0.25% cuts in May, August and December. This allowed councils to place deposits at higher rates than budgeted. Vale achieved a 4.22% nominal rate of return. After adjusting for CPI inflation of 3.3%, the real return was 0.92%.
findings.matters: Finance directors plan investment income as a revenue source; the outperformance shows councils managing cash actively, but the benign conditions that enabled it are transient, and forward forecasts show a return to constraint.
findings.figures: Vale: 4.22% nominal return, 0.92% after inflation; Base Rate fell 0.75% (three 0.25% cuts), ending at 3.75%
findings.quote: The slower cuts in the Base Rate than originally forecast, allowed both councils to place deposits at above budgeted interest rates and generate investment returns above the budget forecasts.

findings.paper_title: Joint AGC outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Vale of White Horse generated £6.401m actual investment income against budgeted £4.342m, outperforming by £2.059m.
findings.detail: Investment returns from treasury balances exceeded forecast by a substantial margin. The outperformance resulted from base rate falling by three 0.25 per cent cuts during the year (ending at 3.75 per cent in March 2026) more slowly than originally forecast, allowing deposits to be placed at above-budgeted rates. After adjusting for 3.3 per cent CPI inflation, the real net return on investments was 0.92 per cent. Overall, including property investments and non-treasury loans, actual investment income was £6.587m against budget of £4.426m.
findings.matters: Lenders assessing council creditworthiness track whether councils can generate income to support their medium-term financial plans independently of council tax and government grant; surplus investment income is a sign of active cash management and balance sheet strength.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse plans to use £3.6m of reserves in 2027/28 against a sustainable £2.9m
news_drafts.lead:
Vale of White Horse District Council's medium-term financial plan (MTFP) projects it will draw £3.6m from its reserves, the money it has put aside, in 2027/28. The sustainable level is £2.9m, leaving a shortfall of £754,000. The figures are in the budget-setting report going to the council's Cabinet on 9 October 2026.

The gap widens in later years, according to the plan the council agreed in February 2026. The shortfall against the sustainable level is projected at £2.1m in 2028/29, £3.3m in 2029/30 and £4.8m in 2030/31. The report says the amount expected to be used in 2027/28 "was much higher than that needed in 2026/27 and would not be in line with the recommended parameters, based on current estimates". Beyond that year, it says, use of reserves "was projected to continue to be unsustainable and outside of the parameters set".

The report says "action will be required by the council to address the increasing budget gap". It adds that the pause in local government reorganisation, the restructuring of councils in the area, means the council now has to deal with the gap sooner than it first expected.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse: all eight key financial audits rated Substantial; cyber security rated Limited
news_drafts.lead:
All eight of the Vale of White Horse's key financial control audits for 2025/26 were completed with a "Substantial" assurance rating, the Joint Audit and Governance Committee was told on 6 October. The audits covered accounts payable, accounts receivable, council tax, the general ledger, business rates, treasury management (how the council borrows and invests its cash), payroll, and housing benefit and council tax reduction claims. Together they produced five management actions, all the lowest priority, and none rated Priority 1 or 2.

The internal audit and risk manager's overall opinion on 2024/25 was that there was "a satisfactory system of governance, risk, internal control", with enhancements recommended in some areas. One audit went the other way: cyber security, including artificial intelligence, was rated "Limited", which the papers say means significant improvement is needed. It produced nine management actions, two of them Priority 1 (fundamental to service integrity), five Priority 2 and two Priority 3.

The external auditor, Bishop Fleming, disclaimed the 2024/25 accounts for both councils, meaning it did not give an opinion on them, as part of wider problems across local audit. Its roadmap aims for qualified accounts for 2025/26 and unqualified for 2026/27, subject to satisfactory progress on "build back" work. The committee also said the number of overdue internal audit recommendations had been "excessive", and recent reports show it falling. Three audits were deferred from the 2025/26 plan: two pending the Ocella replacement project, and one moved to 2027/28.

news_drafts.headline: Vale of White Horse investment returns ahead of budget as deposit rates beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: The Vale of White Horse council expects to receive £1.146m more in investment income than budgeted for 2026–27, driven by higher returns on its treasury deposits, the cabinet heard this week. The council's cash reserves are earning 4.26 per cent on average, outperforming the government's Sterling Overnight Index Average benchmark of 3.74 per cent. However, the council is also forecasting a £698,000 overspend on employee costs in the first quarter, largely because of spending on staff for the local government reorganisation programme, project surveyors and temporary legal cover. A £0.7m underspend on disabled facilities grants, which fund home adaptations for disabled people, is under national review by the Department for Health and Social Care, and the council risks having to return unspent money.
